lessons.title: Nutrients and digestive systems
lessons.html:
Nutrients and digestive systems

A feed miller does not formulate diets, but must understand nutrition well enough to see why specifications, ingredient quality and process control matter. Errors in the mill translate directly into nutrient deficiencies or excesses on farm.

The six nutrient classes

NutrientFunctionMain sources
WaterEvery body process; often limiting firstDrinking water, feed moisture
Energy (carbohydrates, fats)Maintenance, growth, productionMaize, sorghum, wheat, fats and oils
Protein and amino acidsMuscle, eggs, milk, enzymesSoya oilcake, sunflower oilcake, fishmeal, synthetic lysine and methionine
FibreRumen function; gut healthRoughage, bran, hulls
MineralsBone, eggshell, metabolismLimestone, phosphates, salt, trace mineral premix
VitaminsMetabolism and immunityVitamin premix

Amino acids

Animals need specific essential amino acids, not just crude protein. In maize-soya diets for poultry and pigs, lysine and methionine are typically the first limiting amino acids, which is why synthetic forms are added in small, precise amounts. A batching error on these micro-ingredients has a large effect on performance.

Monogastrics and ruminants

  • Monogastrics (poultry, pigs) have a simple stomach. They depend on the diet for essential amino acids and digest fibre poorly. Diets are energy- and amino-acid dense.
  • Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have a rumen where microbes ferment fibre and make microbial protein. They can use roughage and non-protein nitrogen such as urea, but urea must be strictly controlled because excess causes urea poisoning.
  • Horses are hindgut fermenters and are sensitive to some feed additives, such as certain ionophores, that are used safely in other species.

lessons.title: Ingredients, formulation and feed safety
lessons.html:
Ingredients, formulation and feed safety

Ingredient quality

  • Nutrient content of raw materials varies by origin, season and processing. Mills use laboratory and NIR analysis to update ingredient values used in formulation.
  • Mycotoxins, such as aflatoxin and fumonisin in maize, reduce performance and can be toxic. Pigs and poultry are particularly sensitive to some mycotoxins. Screening at intake and binders in the formulation help manage risk.
  • Oilcakes vary in protein and fibre depending on dehulling and oil extraction.
  • Fats can go rancid; antioxidants and storage control matter.

Least-cost formulation

Nutritionists use linear programming software to find the cheapest combination of ingredients that meets all nutrient constraints (energy, digestible amino acids, calcium, phosphorus, fibre, inclusion limits). Because maize and soya prices change with markets and exchange rates, formulations change often. The mill must load the correct, current formulation version and confirm it before production.

Feeding programmes

Different feeds are specified for each production stage: broiler starter, grower and finisher; layer pre-lay and layer phases; pig creep, weaner, grower, finisher, sow lactation and gestation; dairy meal; feedlot starter and finisher; winter and summer licks for veld cattle. Feeding the wrong product at the wrong stage causes losses on farm, so labelling and dispatch accuracy matter as much as production.

Regulation and labelling

Under Act 36 of 1947, farm feeds are registered and must carry a label with the registration number, guaranteed analysis and directions for use. Medicated feeds must follow the registered product conditions, including withdrawal periods stated on the label.

Key points

  • Feeds supply water, energy, protein, fibre, minerals and vitamins.
  • Essential amino acids such as lysine and methionine are added precisely.
  • Ruminants ferment fibre and can use urea, which must be tightly controlled.
  • Mycotoxins and variable ingredient quality are major risks.
  • Least-cost formulations change often; always confirm the current version.
  • Feeds are registered and labelled under Act 36 of 1947.
